title: Search Open Technical Databases: CDNs
summary: A content delivery network keeps copies of a site's content on many edge servers and answers each request from the location nearest the user. That arrangement hides the origin server address, but it also creates a second copy of the site on infrastructure the organisation does not fully control. An adversary studies the delivery network by resolving host names, reading response headers, and testing whether the origin address still accepts direct connections that skip the delivery layer. Typical findings are staging or administrative paths hosted without the authentication used on the main site, and cached files that were never meant to be public. In delivery network access logs the enumeration appears as many requests for unusual paths from a small set of addresses, a pattern ordinary visitors do not produce.

beginner.definition: A content delivery network is a group of servers around the world. These servers store copies of a website so it loads faster. The same setup can create a second, less protected copy of the site. This technique means an attacker studies that second copy.
beginner.whyItMatters: The main website may be well protected while the copy on the delivery network is not. Old test pages and login screens sometimes stay there by mistake. An attacker finds these and uses them as an easier way in. The traffic looks like normal website visits, so it is hard to spot. Checking that copy is part of keeping your site safe.
howItWorks: The attacker resolves your host names and notes which addresses belong to a delivery network.
They read the response headers to learn which delivery provider you use.
They request unusual paths such as admin, backup, or staging on the same host name.
They look for an origin address that still answers requests sent directly.
They save cached files and error pages that reveal internal host names.
They use the findings to plan a later compromise or a fake login page.
beginner.example: Imagine a chain of corner shops that all sell the same goods from one central warehouse. The shop shelves are tidy and staffed, but the warehouse loading bay is often left open. A thief studies the bay, not the shop front. Your delivery network is the shop front, and your origin server is the bay. Attackers usually look for the loading bay first.
takeaways: Protect the origin server so it refuses traffic that did not come through the delivery network.
Check the delivery network for old test pages and unprotected login screens.
Confirm what your site returns for unusual paths such as admin or backup.

objectives: Explain how a content delivery network both hides and exposes origin infrastructure.
Describe how response headers and cache behaviour support reconnaissance.
Identify common delivery network misconfigurations that leak content.
Explain how to restrict origin access so only the delivery provider can reach it.
Recognise host and path enumeration patterns in delivery network access logs.
